sections.h2: What to check first in Upper Arlington
sections.html: Upper Arlington is a planned suburb on the northwest side of Columbus. A sale here turns on lot layout, school boundaries and a few city rules that older houses trigger. The city sits entirely in Franklin County, with the Scioto River along its west edge. The population is about 35,893, down from 36,800 in 2020. This page covers what the city inspects, what the county handles and what Ohio expects from a seller on paper, so you can judge how fast a sale can move.

sections.h2: Two housing stocks on one map
sections.html:
Two brothers who developed real estate bought the first 840 acres south of present-day Lane Avenue in 1913 and followed a Garden City plan with deep setbacks, parks and separate zones for shops and apartments. The village incorporated in 1918, and cityhood came on February 8, 1941. Annexations, mostly between the late 1940s and 1960, built out the rest. The result:

  • South of Lane Avenue, the Old Arlington district holds Colonial and English Revival houses. The district was added to the National Register in 1985.
  • North of Lane, post-war tracts such as River Ridge follow ordinary street grids with ranch houses, and houses built from the 1960s on grew larger.

Which side of Lane Avenue your house sits on decides which city rules you meet first.

This is a pricey, owner-heavy suburb, so buyers compare your house against a high-priced local market. Condition and presentation carry weight.

  • About 79.4% of housing units are lived in by their owners.
  • The typical owner-occupied house is valued at $595,600.
  • Monthly ownership costs run $3,189 for households with a mortgage and $1,284 for those without.
  • The city holds 14,330 households averaging 2.52 people.
  • Household income at the midpoint is $155,167.
  • Roughly 88.2% of residents were in the same home twelve months earlier.

The Upper Arlington City School District serves the whole city, and its high school was rebuilt in 2021. Downtown Columbus and the Ohio State campus are a short drive away.

It can matter if the buyer plans to tear the house down. In 2009 City Council adopted rules meant to discourage, without prohibiting, total demolition of historically significant homes. A six-month delay period gives owners and the city time to look for alternatives, and the rules appear in Articles 5, 6 and 7 of the Unified Development Ordinance.

The city's GIS maps show which properties are identified as historically significant, and Community Development posts a Guide to Demolition in the Historic District along with an owner statement and a demolition sign affidavit. Selling a house south of Lane Avenue to a builder or investor? Tell the buyer up front and ask Community Development whether your parcel is flagged.

sections.h2: City offices for permits and exterior complaints
sections.html:
Community Development runs three divisions: Planning, Building and Code Compliance. The office at 3600 Tremont Road keeps weekday hours of 8 am to 5 pm. The main line is 614-583-5070, and inspections are 614-583-5080.

Exterior upkeep is mostly complaint driven. High grass and weeds, flaking paint, illegal temporary signs, excess lighting, trash and debris, and noise are the common violations. A confirmed complaint brings a written Notice of Violation with a re-inspection date, which an officer may extend for substantial progress, bad weather or other mitigating circumstances. Most violations carry a maximum of $150 per offense per day, and a few are fourth degree misdemeanors with a $250 maximum fine and up to 30 days in jail.

sections.h2: Clearing out a cluttered or dated house
sections.html:
Bulk items go to the curb by 7 am on your regular collection day, and mattresses and box springs must be wrapped in plastic. Large appliances and anything containing Freon may cost extra, so ask Local Waste Services at 614-409-9375, option 2, before you set them out.

  • One garage or yard sale per residence is allowed in any six-month period, for no more than three consecutive days, with no permit.
  • A plumbing permit is needed to install or replace a boiler, water heater or water meter, or any time supply or waste lines change.
  • Decks, fences, driveway replacements, detached garages and pools each appear as their own permit type in the online system.

Finished basements, new decks and swapped water heaters are the usual places a permit gap shows up. Pull the permit history first and close any gap before you accept an offer.

Because the whole city is in Franklin County, one auditor handles both topics. Landlords file owner or manager contact details with that office under Ohio Revised Code 5323.02, within 60 days of the notice that follows a property transfer or of receiving a tax bill. A property left unfiled draws a $150 fine for each tax year, and an owner living outside Ohio has to name an Ohio contact.

A value complaint also starts at the auditor. ORC 5715.19 sets the cutoff at the end of March after the tax year, or the day first-half collection closes if that is later. The Board of Revision looks at the property's value only, so the tax bill itself is outside its scope.

Franklin's standard Homestead Exemption helps lower-income owners who turn 65 by year-end or are permanently and totally disabled. An enhanced version for owners with a 100% service-connected disability rating shields $50,000 of appraised value from tax and has no income test.

sections.h2: What an Ohio seller must hand the buyer
sections.html:
Ohio's residential disclosure statute, section 5302.30, has the seller complete a state form about the condition of the property and pass a signed copy to the buyer early. If it arrives after the contract, the buyer gets a short window to back out, and that window also applies when the form never shows up.

Answer each item honestly and amend the form if facts change. Where you truly don't know an answer, the statute allows a good faith estimate.

The trade is time against price. An agent listing puts the house in front of owner-occupant buyers, which means showings and waiting on a lender. A direct as-is purchase can shorten the wait, and the offer drops by whatever repairs the buyer absorbs.

  • Get each offer in writing with the closing date, who covers closing costs and which repairs are excluded.
  • Request proof of funds before you sign.
  • Look up the permit history and any open exterior complaint before listing, since both can push a closing date.

A buyer who pays cash and skips the lender removes the loan approval step, but the city and county tasks above stay on your list. Do them in this order: permit history, open complaints, disclosure form, then the offer.

faqs.q: Does Upper Arlington require a permit for a deck or fence?
faqs.a: Yes. Decks and fences each appear as residential permit types in the city's online system. Call Community Development at 614-583-5070 before work begins and confirm that earlier projects on your house were closed out.

faqs.q: Can a buyer tear down my Old Arlington house?
faqs.a: Often yes, after a delay. The 2009 rules in the Unified Development Ordinance set a six-month delay period for total demolition of historically significant homes. Ask Community Development whether your parcel is identified in the city's GIS maps.

faqs.q: Do I need to register a rental house in Upper Arlington before selling it?
faqs.a: The registration comes from the county auditor, not the city, and rests on Ohio Revised Code 5323.02. A missing filing carries a $150 fine per tax year, so update the contact record before closing. The auditor's line is 614-525-4663.

faqs.q: When can I dispute my home's value?
faqs.a: File with the Franklin County Auditor by the end of March after the tax year, or the first-half collection deadline when that is later. The Board of Revision, at 614-525-3913, rules on value only.

faqs.q: Who completes the Ohio property disclosure form?
faqs.a: The seller does. Section 5302.30 covers most sales of homes with up to four units, and some transfers, such as gifts to a spouse or a relative in the direct line, fall outside it.
